learn.title: Walking the chain
learn.body: To visit every node, start at head and keep moving to `next` until you reach NULL. A temporary pointer does the walking, so head is never changed.

learn.title: Print every value
learn.body: The loop is the standard shape: start, test for NULL, step to next.

learn.title: Searching
learn.body: Return 1 if value v is in the list. This looks at nodes one by one, so a long list takes longer.

learn.title: Freeing the list
learn.body: Save `next` before freeing, because a freed node must not be read.

learn.title: Why save next
learn.body: Freeing `l` first and then reading `l->next` is a bug.
steps: `free(l)` hands the node back to the system
So copy `l->next` into `nx` first, then free

questions.prompt: Why walk with a separate pointer `p`?
choices: So head still points to the start
questions.explanation: If you moved head itself, you would lose the beginning of the list.

questions.prompt: When does the loop `p != NULL` stop?
choices: When p has moved past the last node
questions.explanation: The last node's next is NULL, so p becomes NULL after it.

questions.prompt: To step to the next node, write p = p\_\_next.
questions.explanation: p is a pointer, so use the arrow to read its field.

choices: A freed node must not be read
questions.explanation: After free the memory is no longer yours. Reading it is undefined behaviour.

questions.prompt: A list holds 4, 8, 15. How many nodes does `show` visit?
questions.explanation: One for each node, then it stops at NULL.

questions.prompt: Searching for a value in a list of 1000 nodes may need to look at...
questions.explanation: A list has no index, so the search walks from the front.
The check comes before using p, and the move comes last.
